diagnostic_evidence.quote:
The exact solution is chosen to have non-trivial boundary conditions:
\[
u(x) = \sin(x) e^x.
\]
The forcing function $f(x)$ and Dirichlet boundary data are derived from this exact solution.

issues.failure_explanation: The defined system uses all N equations to enforce the differential equation and imposes no Dirichlet data at the physical endpoints. The basis vanishes only at the extended endpoints, not at 0 and L. Thus this construction does not define a solver for the stated physical boundary-value problems, especially the experiment advertised as having nontrivial boundary data.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: The discrete system must be redesigned to enforce the physical boundary conditions, for example by replacing suitable interior equations with boundary equations, and the stability and convergence analysis must then be redone for that altered matrix.
issues.overall_effect: Claims that the scheme solves the stated elliptic boundary-value problems, and convergence claims for its computed solution, are unsupported by the actual construction.
issues.title: The collocation construction omits the physical boundary conditions
issues.why_classification: The repair changes the central discrete operator and requires new stability analysis rather than a local amendment.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Our uniform grid for $x_k$ makes the angles $\theta_k$ an arithmetic progression. The nodes $\xi_j = \cos\theta_j$ are therefore cosines of equispaced angles.

issues.failure_explanation: For fixed positive extension, the angles lie in a strict subinterval of (0,pi), where sin(theta) is bounded away from zero. Consequently the map xi=cos(theta) has nonvanishing derivative throughout the interpolation interval, so equispaced theta-nodes remain quasi-uniform at the xi-endpoints rather than having Chebyshev's quadratic endpoint clustering. The cited logarithmic Chebyshev-node estimate therefore does not apply; polynomial interpolation at such quasi-uniform nodes can have exponentially growing Lebesgue constants.

failure_location.quote: While not identical to classical Chebyshev points, such nodes exhibit the same characteristic clustering near the interval endpoints. It is a well-established result in approximation theory that the Lebesgue constant for polynomial interpolation at these nodes exhibits logarithmic growth

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a valid degree-dependent Lebesgue estimate for the actual cosine-transformed uniform grid must replace the inapplicable Chebyshev estimate, with all dependent multidimensional and dichotomy claims revised accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed logarithmic stability of the one-dimensional basis and the product logarithmic bound in multiple dimensions are unproved, undermining the stated stability dichotomy.
issues.title: Logarithmic basis bound uses a false characterization of the transformed nodes
issues.why_classification: The asserted logarithmic rate is the substantive conclusion and cannot be retained by a local correction; the actual node geometry requires a different global analysis and may yield exponential growth.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The matrix $\mat{W}(\delta)$, when scaled, converges to $\mat{M}$.

issues.failure_explanation: Ill-conditioning of the coefficients in a degenerating basis is not by itself ill-conditioning of the interpolation operator. The Lagrange functions involve the product of the evaluation row with W^{-1}; the same degeneration in the evaluation row can cancel the growth of W^{-1}. No lower bound on a Lagrange function or the Lebesgue constant is established. For example, for fixed N the nearly dependent sine functions can be recombined into successively scaled polynomial-like functions, so convergence of the raw basis matrix to a singular matrix does not force the interpolation spaces themselves to become unstable.

failure_location.quote: The smallest singular value $\sigma_{\min}(\mat{W}(\delta))$ must tend to zero. The Lebesgue constant, which depends on the norm of the inverse of the collocation matrix, must therefore be unbounded as $\delta \to \infty$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, the paper must directly estimate the cardinal functions or exhibit interpolation data whose interpolant norm diverges as delta tends to infinity.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted large-extension instability and the claimed existence of an optimal extension parameter are unsupported.
issues.title: Near-singularity of a chosen basis matrix does not imply divergence of the Lebesgue constant
issues.why_classification: The sole argument proves only coefficient ill-conditioning, and a fundamentally different interpolation-operator argument is needed to retain the theorem.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We can assume without loss of generality that $\alpha$ is an irrational number.

The coefficients $a_j$ in the continued fraction expansion are unbounded for almost all real numbers $\alpha$. Thus, we can choose an infinite subsequence of indices $\{j_m\}_{m=1}^\infty$ such that $a_{j_m+1} \ge e^{q_{j_m}}$.

The total error $\Delta_k = \frac{\theta_k(N)}{\pi} - m_k$ can be shown to be bounded by:
\[
|\Delta_k| \le C \cdot q_j \cdot |\epsilon_j|
\]

issues.failure_explanation: Successive phases have the fixed increment theta_{k+1}-theta_k = pi N L/((N-1)(L+2delta)), which tends to pi L/(L+2delta), strictly between 0 and pi. If every sine value were exponentially small, each successive phase would have to be exponentially close to an integer multiple of pi, forcing their increment to be exponentially close to an integer multiple of pi, contradicting that limiting increment. The appendix also improperly discards rational parameter ratios, infers exponentially large partial quotients from mere unboundedness, and leaves the claimed integer approximation as an unproved assertion.

failure_location.quote:
There exist an infinite subsequence of integers $\{N_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ and a constant $c > 0$ (depending on $L$ and $\delta$) such that
\[
\max_{k \in \{0, \dots, N_j-1\}} |\sin(\theta_k(N_j))| < e^{-cN_j}
\]

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, the false lemma must be withdrawn and any Poisson lower bound must be proved by a different mechanism consistent with the nonzero phase increment.
issues.overall_effect: The exponential subsequence lower bound and hence the supplied proof of super-polynomial Poisson growth fail.
issues.title: The simultaneous exponential-smallness lemma is arithmetically impossible
issues.why_classification: The lemma's conclusion is false, not merely insufficiently justified, and it is the decisive input to the Poisson instability theorem.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: A careful analysis shows that for nodes in $[a,b] \subset (0,L)$ and evaluation points $x \in (-\delta, 0)$, the integral is bounded by $C/K$ for a constant $C$ that depends on the geometry ($L, \delta, a, b$) but not on the degree $M$.

issues.failure_explanation: Remez and analytic-extrapolation constants from a proper subinterval to a larger interval necessarily grow with degree; trigonometric polynomials can increasingly concentrate on the extension while remaining small on I. Likewise, Lagrange functions evaluated outside their node interval generally grow exponentially with degree, rather than satisfying the asserted C/K bound. Thus the continuous norm on the extended domain cannot be bounded by the physical-domain norm with a degree-independent constant.

failure_location.quote:
Then there exists a constant $C_R$, which depends only on the geometry of $I$ and $\tilde{I}$ but is independent of the polynomial degree $M$, such that for any $g \in P_M$:
\[
\norm{g}_{L^2(\tilde{I})} \le C_R \norm{g}_{L^2(I)}.
\]

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, the correct degree-dependent restriction or Remez constant must be derived and propagated through the singular-value and Lebesgue estimates.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed N-independent lower bound on the collocation matrix singular value, and all constant-, variable-, and multidimensional polynomial stability results derived from it, lose a central step.
issues.title: The degree-independent nested-interval Remez inequality is false
issues.why_classification: Correcting the inequality may introduce exponential degree dependence, destroying the advertised polynomial stability and requiring new proof architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: The space of general trigonometric polynomials of degree N has dimension 2N+1, while only N samples are taken. Hence there is a nonzero T_N vanishing at all N grid points, making the left side zero while its L2 norm is positive. An M=O(N) statement requires a specified bandwidth-to-sampling ratio and appropriate periodic geometry; neither is supplied.

failure_location.quote:
For functions in the space containing $\{L[u_N]\}$, which have degree $M=O(N)$, an equivalence between the discrete and continuous $L^2$ norms holds. Specifically, there exists a constant $c_1' > 0$ independent of $N$ such that:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N} |T_N(x_i)|^2 \ge c_1' \norm{T_N}_{L^2(I)}^2.
\]

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a valid sampling theorem for the precise N-dimensional image space L[V_N], with the actual grid and constants, must replace this false general statement.
issues.overall_effect: The discrete-to-continuous lower bound used to prove uniformly positive minimal singular values is unavailable, so the polynomial Lebesgue bounds do not follow.
issues.title: The stated sampling inequality is false at the claimed sampling density
issues.why_classification: The required lower sampling bound is central to every discrete stability proof and cannot be repaired merely by changing a constant.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The sum $\max_{x \in I} \sum_{j=1}^N \abs{\phi_j(x)}$ is bounded by $O(N^3)$ because the continuously differentiable function $k(x)$ is bounded on the compact interval $I$.
Let $T_M(x)$ be a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $M$ on the interval $I=(0,L)$.

issues.failure_explanation: For variable k, L[u_N]=-u_N''+k(x)u_N' is generally not a trigonometric polynomial of degree O(N), even when u_N is. Therefore neither trigonometric-polynomial norm lemma applies to the quantity used in the proof. Their asserted independence of k does not cure this hypothesis violation.

failure_location.quote: It relies on the norm-equivalence results of Lemma~\ref{lem:norm_equivalence} and Lemma~\ref{lem:mz_inequality}, which are independent of $k(x)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: A new norming or sampling result must be proved for the spaces -V_N''+kV_N', with quantitative dependence on k, or the theorem must be restricted to coefficient classes preserving finite bandwidth.
issues.overall_effect: Even if the two norm lemmas were corrected for bandlimited functions, the paper would still lack the sampling and restriction estimates needed for variable convection and general multidimensional fields.
issues.title: Variable-coefficient images are outside the trigonometric-polynomial lemmas
issues.why_classification: The theorem applies its principal tools outside their function class, and extending them to arbitrary C1 multipliers requires a new substantive argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: If the convection coefficient $k(x) \in C^1(\tilde{I})$ satisfies the condition $\norm{k'}_{L^\infty(\tilde{I})} < 2/C_P^2$, then the operator is coercive on $H_0^1(\tilde{I})$.

issues.failure_explanation: A function assumed only to belong to C1(I) has no defined derivative or norm on the larger interval tilde I, so the theorem's condition is ill-defined and the continuous coercivity lemma's C1(tilde I) hypothesis is not met.

failure_location.quote: Let the convection coefficient $k(x) \in C^1(I)$ satisfy the coercivity condition $\norm{k'}_{L^\infty(\tilde{I})} < 2/C_P^2$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require k to be defined in C1(tilde I), or explicitly supply an extension having the stated derivative bound.
issues.overall_effect: The stated variable-coefficient theorem is not well-defined for its advertised coefficient class.
issues.title: The variable-coefficient hypothesis uses k outside its stated domain
issues.why_classification: This particular defect has a short local hypothesis correction that preserves the intended theorem, independently of the theorem's other proof failures.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The stated convergence rate then follows from the fundamental approximation properties of spectral methods for functions of finite Sobolev regularity.
A Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_N$ that grows polynomially (or slower) with $N$ ensures the stability and, ultimately, the convergence of the method.

issues.failure_explanation: Sobolev regularity gives a best-approximation rate, not automatically the same rate for the collocation solution. The proof establishes neither consistency plus stability nor a quasi-optimality estimate connecting u_N to the best approximation. In particular, the paper's own polynomial Lebesgue bounds would generally multiply approximation errors by an N-dependent factor, so they do not justify the unchanged exponent r+2.

failure_location.quote:
Consequently, the $L^2$-error of the spectral approximation is bounded by:
\[
\norm{u - u_N}_{L^2(I)} = O(N^{-(r+2)}).
\]

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a boundary-consistent collocation error estimate must combine approximation, residual consistency, and the actual stability growth, with the resulting rate stated accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The precise algebraic convergence guarantee and the claimed direct correspondence between coefficient regularity and computed collocation error are unsupported.
issues.title: The convergence rate is asserted without a stable or quasi-optimal discretization argument
issues.why_classification: Retaining the exact advertised rate requires a new convergence theory; using only the supplied polynomial stability can materially worsen the rate.
